framing: Write the rules, then attack them
paragraphs: Human reviewers don't scale to every new failure, and they won't think of every trick an attacker will. So teams write their rules down, use them to generate training data, and then try to break the result.

Constitutional AI turns written principles into revised answers and AI comparisons. Red teaming attacks what comes out. Both rely on judges that make mistakes, so honest counts matter as much as the method. And neither one decides who may read what.

An infrastructure assistant gives us public requests, private ones, and attempts to talk past the rules. You'll follow a bad draft to a revised answer, follow AI labels to a reward model, count attacks and useful answers with nothing hidden, and see where enforcement has to live.
The last two chapters showed how labels move a policy. This one asks how those labels get made and how they get challenged. A little Python and basic probability will carry you through.
outcomes: Say exactly what each stage of Constitutional AI trains.
Report attacks with coverage, unresolved cases, and what happened to permitted tasks.
Tell a model's bad proposal from an effect the application actually executed.
question: Which conclusion in your safety report would change if a missing judgment turned out to be a violation?
